messages.subject: Re: Width of subclasses
messages.body_plain:
Hi Theodor,
I think you could accomplish what you want using the subclass option.  See:

http://gking.harvard.edu/node/4355/rbuild_documentation/Additional_Arguments_f2.html

"subclass: either a scalar specifying the number of subclasses, or a vector of probabilities bounded between 0 and 1, which create quantiles of the distance measure using the units in the group specified by sub.by (default = subclass = 6)."

So if you can figure out what quantiles the cutpoints you want correspond to you should be able to specify it that way.

Liz

messages.subject: sensitivity analysis
messages.body_plain:
How can I do a sensitivity analysis utilizing a matched dataframe derived from MatchIt? 

//M
messages.body_snippet:
How can I do a sensitivity analysis utilizing a matched dataframe derived from MatchIt? 

//M

messages.subject: Re: sensitivity analysis
messages.body_plain:
Two ways:

(A)  If by sensitivity analysis you mean "sensitivity analysis as I would
with a static dataset", just do as you would have done with the static
dataset.  The robustness measures will depend on the model that you are
fitting, irrespective of whether the data are static or matched.

(B)  If you mean "how sensitive are my treatment effects to the specific
matched pairs constructed from a particular matching algorithm", then you
can do one of two things:
   (1)  Generate several matched datasets using a given matching algorithm,
estimate your model separately on each, then combine the results using the
Rubin rules (Zelig will do this for you automatically for most models); or
   (2)   Repeat (1) using a different matching algorithm (e.g., if you were
using propensity scores without mahalanobis distance calipers, add the
calipers, or use genetic matching or use .... any of the other options) and
see if you get the same substantive results.

Matching is a NP hard problem -- there is no "right" answer, but if the
substantive results are there, you should be able to obtain similar findings
with different matching algorithms.

Yours,
Olivia

messages.subject: Re: sensitivity analysis
messages.body_plain:
No, unfortunately there is no built-in sensitivity analysis function in MatchIt, in part because of the range of types of matching methods MatchIt can accommodate.

You might want to see the bottom of my webpage on software for matching methods, which lists software that is available; it would be very possible to run many of these on the results you obtain from MatchIt.

http://www.biostat.jhsph.edu/~estuart/propensityscoresoftware.html

Liz

   (1)  Generate several matched datasets using a given matching algorithm, estimate your model separately on each, then combine the results using the Rubin rules (Zelig will do this for you automatically for most models); or
   (2)   Repeat (1) using a different matching algorithm (e.g., if you were using propensity scores without mahalanobis distance calipers, add the calipers, or use genetic matching or use .... any of the other options) and see if you get the same substantive results.

messages.body_plain:
Thx..This seems to work. 


pseudocode:
pm<-matchit(Tr~A+B+C+D,method="cem",data=p2)
p.match<-match.data(pm)

hlsens(p.match$Y[p.match$Tr==1],p.match$Y[p.match$Tr==0])


//M
